A new startup called CiteProof has launched an AI-powered tool designed to detect fabricated or erroneous legal citations in documents, addressing a growing concern in the legal profession about AI-generated content containing fake references.

The tool analyzes legal briefs, motions, and academic papers to identify citations that don't exist, have been misattributed, or reference incorrect holdings. Early users report that the system catches issues that would typically require hours of manual verification.

## The Citation Problem

Legal professionals have expressed increasing concern about AI-generated legal documents containing hallucinations—fabricated case citations that appear legitimate but don't exist. In high-stakes litigation, such errors can result in sanctions, delayed proceedings, and reputational damage.

"Law firms are adopting AI tools at record pace, but the verification burden has shifted from writing to checking," explained a legal technology consultant. "CiteProof addresses a real pain point."

## How It Works

The system combines large language models trained on millions of legal documents with a proprietary database of verified case law. When analyzing a document, it cross-references each citation against primary sources and flags potential issues with confidence scores.

The tool integrates with common legal practice management systems and can process documents in bulk, making it suitable for law firm libraries and litigation teams reviewing large document collections.

## Market Response

CiteProof joins a growing ecosystem of AI tools targeting legal industry pain points. Competitors include Premonition (acquired by Relativity) and several academic research projects focused on legal citation verification.

The company has announced a freemium model for individual practitioners while targeting enterprise deployments with larger law firms and corporate legal departments.
